symb.description:
**SymbolicSymphony** is a framework developed in **Unreal Engine 5.8** aimed at recreating *Sonic Unleashed*. Initially one of my first programming experiences, it has been continually updated to leverage modern technologies.

### Core Architecture
- **C++ & Blueprint Integration**: Developed robustly in C++ while remaining fully extensible via Blueprints.
- **Custom Asynchronous Loading**: A flexible C++ subsystem dedicated to async loading.
- **Memory Management**: Heavy manual control over object lifetime using `TObjectPtr`, weak references, and soft references.
- **Decoupled Garbage Collection**: Memory and lifecycle management are scoped directly to components and subsystems to ensure strict architectural decoupling.

day.introduction: The day sections feature Sonic's classic high-speed platforming gameplay.
day.presentation:
### General Overview
Inspired by daytime gameplay from *Sonic Unleashed*, focusing on a high-speed, fluid, and responsive experience in **Unreal Engine 5**.

### Custom Ability System
- Custom **C++ component** heavily inspired by Unreal's **Gameplay Ability System (GAS)**.
- Utilizes a **tag-driven architecture**. Multiple independent ability scripts work in harmony, dynamically controlling each other's execution states, cancellations, and permissions via **Gameplay Tags**.
- Abilities are configured through **Data Assets**, allowing their behavior, rules, and properties to be easily customized.
- Uses **delegates** to broadcast state or property changes to other systems asynchronously.
- Unifies both **movement mechanics and gameplay abilities** under a single flexible system.
- Works seamlessly with both **C++ and Blueprints**, allowing abilities to be created and configured directly in the editor.
- Designed to make it easy to add new abilities while keeping the codebase **modular, reusable, and scalable**.

### Daytime Gameplay / 3D Platforming
- **Custom physics**: Slope handling, wall jumps, and inertia-based speed.
- Object interaction managed via a **dedicated state machine**.
- **Quick Time Events (QTEs)** integrated for cinematic, interactive moments.
- **Dynamic camera**: Spline-guided transitions and cinematic angles to enhance the perception of speed.

### Interface and User Experience
- Custom **C++ UI Subsystem** acting as a layer over **Common UI**.
- Dynamically activates UI elements based on **Gameplay Tag channels**.
- Heavily utilizes **asynchronous loading** via **soft references** for optimized resource management and smooth UI animations.

night.introduction: The night sections feature a one-versus-all combat system combined with platforming challenges.
night.presentation:
### General Overview
Inspired by the **Werehog**, this gameplay loop combines heavy combat, platforming, and muscular movement, balancing raw power with animal agility.

### Visual System
- Custom **shell system** for fur rendering.
- Fully optimized for UE5, leveraging **Nanite** and **Lumen** for density and lighting.

### Combat System
Built entirely on the **Custom Ability System**, enabling players to:
- Grab and throw enemies.
- Execute and extend complex combos.
- Trigger **QTEs** for cinematic contextual finishers.

### Locomotion and Movement
A dedicated locomotion mode manages varied movements like climbing, swinging, and cliff traversal with physics-based weight and responsiveness.

### Defense and AI
- **Shield system** for blocking and deflecting incoming attacks.
- AI driven by **State Trees** (upgraded from Behavior Trees) for maximum performance and responsiveness.
night.fur:
### Shell System
A custom **shell-based fur system** created as a highly performant alternative to the demanding Unreal Groom System.

It works by stacking multiple slightly scaled copies of the mesh (layers) using a fur texture and transparency to create depth and volume. This provides excellent visual fidelity and runtime performance for stylized rendering. This technique was also adapted for my *Gestalt Therapy* project.
night.finisher:
### Finishers
Combat includes **finisher sequences** triggered when an enemy is stunned.

During the stunned state, a **random QTE prompt** appears:
- **Success**: Plays a cinematic finisher animation that instantly defeats the enemy.
- **Failure**: The player loses health and combo/style gauge, adding risk and tension.

This rewards precision and timing while keeping combat dynamic.
night.loco:
### Locomotion System
Designed for full traversal flexibility while keeping movements fluid and reactive.

- Supports **wall climbing**, **cliff movement**, **swinging**, and **slacklining**.
- Uses a dedicated **Control Rig** and **Inverse Kinematics (IK)** to dynamically deform arms and align hands with the environment.
- Managed by a robust **state machine** for smooth blending between traversal states.
- Swinging allows **360° freedom**, letting players input an **impulse** to control ejection speed and direction.

globe.presentation:
### Interactive UI
The **globe** serves as the main interface for level selection, combining interactive 3D navigation with immersive visual feedback.

### Navigation and Selection
- Levels are selected geographically by **country or region**.
- **Visual progression**: Scattered pieces of the planet gradually reassemble as the player advances, symbolizing story progression and world restoration.

ges.description:
## Gestalt Therapy

### General Overview
**Gestalt Therapy** is a virtual reality experience developed during a credited internship in South Korea. Its goal is to help players relax by interacting with a virtual animal created using **Unreal Engine 5.6**.

### Pipeline and Development
- The animal pipeline is highly modular, allowing multiple animals to be integrated and easily customized.
- Project developed with **VHex Lab**, a South Korean laboratory specializing in psychological games.
- Developed using **Blueprint** and **C++**.

### Interactions and Physics
- Users can **pet a virtual dog** using hand tracking provided by the movement system.
- Custom physical interactions and real-time shader effects simulate realistic fur movement.
- Dynamic physics allows the animal to react naturally to the environment and to petting.

fur.description:
## Interactive Fur

### General Overview
As in my previous project **Symbolic Symphony**, this experience features an animal with fur, but with a **unique twist**: the fur is **fully interactive** and moves naturally in the **direction of the touch**. The player can **pet the animal**, whose body reacts physically, creating a calming and immersive experience.

### Dog Physics
- The virtual dog moves and reacts naturally thanks to its **Physics Body** in **Unreal Engine 5**.
- Limbs, tail, and body respond to player interactions and environmental forces.
- No pre-defined animations are needed, providing a dynamic and realistic experience.

### Technical Explanation
- Vertex colors control fur length and direction in the shader.
- The red channel indicates the main direction, allowing natural and dynamic fur movement.
- The creation pipeline remains fast and flexible, making it easy to generate a wide variety of animals.

ia.arch:
## Model Architecture

The model is based on a **Residual Network (ResNet)** architecture tailored for image restoration. Instead of predicting the original image directly, it learns the **residual** the difference between the compressed and the uncompressed version.

Each residual block includes:
- Two 2D convolutional layers
- Batch normalization
- ReLU activation
- A **skip connection** to improve gradient flow

This design ensures stable training and better recovery of fine details.

```python
return torch.clamp(x, 0, 1)
```

The output tensor is clamped between 0 and 1 to maintain valid intensity values.
ia.drawback:
## Training and Results

I trained the model for several epochs using a loss function combining **MSE** and **SSIM**, weighted at 0.2 and 0.8. This balance ensures both pixel-level accuracy and structural consistency.

```python
mseLoss = F.mse_loss(prediction, target)
ssIMLoss = 1 - ssim(prediction, target, data_range=1.0)
return 0.2 * mseLoss + 0.8 * ssIMLoss
```

The results show a **significant reduction in compression artifacts**. Although the **PSNR** may slightly decrease, the restored images appear smoother and more natural.

Under **extreme compression** (JPEG quality ≈ 2), the output tends to look softer due to the irreversible loss of fine details.

### Conclusion
This project demonstrates the efficiency of **residual networks** for restoring degraded JPEG images. The combined **MSE + SSIM** loss provides a balanced compromise between pixel fidelity and perceptual quality while highlighting the limitations of aggressive compression.

engine.description:
## 3D Rendering Engine - Lighting, Transformations and Camera

This project explores the fundamentals of a 3D rendering engine, including **directional lighting**, **back-face culling**, **geometric transformations**, and **camera projections**.

### Lighting and Culling

1. Addition of a **directional light source** in *view space*, using a **diffuse lighting model** to illuminate solid triangles.
2. Implementation of a **back-face culling toggle**, revealing visual artifacts when culling is disabled.
3. **Triangle picking** system: when a visible triangle is hovered, it becomes highlighted and the **3D coordinates** of the surface point are displayed.

### Transformations

The engine supports full **3D object transformations**:

- **Translation**, **rotation**, and **scaling** using transformation matrices.
- Multiple rotation representations: **Euler angles**, **axis-angle**, and **quaternions**.
- Smooth return to the initial orientation using **LERP** for matrix rotations and **SLERP** for quaternions, demonstrating their shortest-path interpolation.

### Projection and Camera

Supports both **orthographic** and **perspective projections**, with dynamic switching between modes.

An **orbit camera** based on **spherical coordinates** provides smooth and intuitive navigation around 3D objects.

triangulation.description:
## Triangulation

### Implemented Algorithms

- **Naive Triangulation**  
- **Delaunay Triangulation**  
- **Incremental Delaunay**  
- **Voronoi Diagrams**

### Purpose

These algorithms subdivide a set of points into **optimized triangles**, useful for **mesh generation**, **geometry processing**, and **surface modeling**.

convexhull.description:
## Convex Hull

### Implemented Algorithms

- **Extreme Edge**  
- **Jarvis March (Gift Wrapping)**  
- **Graham Scan**

### Purpose

These methods compute the **minimal boundary** enclosing a set of points. The convex hull is a key structure in **collision detection**, **shape analysis**, and **geometry simplification**.

point.description:
## Point Inside Polygon

### Methods Used

- **Convex polygon:** Direction-based edge checking.  
- **Non-convex polygon:** **Edge intersection counting** method.

### Functionality

The algorithm automatically detects whether the polygon is convex or not and applies the corresponding method to determine if the point lies within the polygon's surface.

powder.role: Group Project - Scene creation, UI, Base Classes for elements (Solid/Liquid/Gas), Cell, Weather API fetch
powder.description:
## Elements - Powder

### Purpose
Simulation of falling sand or powder particles with physics interaction and unique behaviors for each element type.

### Architecture
- Each element derives from the **Cell** class.  
- The abstract **update()** method allows each element to have its own rules, avoiding downcasting and simplifying engine logic.
- Example: sand, water, and steam have different update behaviors.

### Grid
- The **grid separates drawing from physics**, allowing cells larger than a pixel and independent cell sizing.
- Each update computes the grid physics first, then updates screen pixels according to the cell size.

### Background
- Background is updated via an **API request** to fetch the current weather.  
- A **convolutional blur** is applied and placed on a **separate layer**, preventing interference with foreground particle rendering.

class.description:
## Element Classes

### Cell
- Base class for all elements.  
- Contains the abstract **update()** method to define specific behavior.

### Solid
- Parent class for all solid elements.
- **MoveableSolid**: solids that can move (e.g., sand, rock).  
- **StaticSolid**: fixed elements in the scene (e.g., wall, terrain).

### Liquid
- Class for liquids (e.g., water).
- Can transform into gas after a certain time or under certain conditions.
- Interaction with terrain: water on dirt can create life.

### Gas
- Class for gases (e.g., steam).
- Can condense into liquid depending on conditions.

### Physical Behavior
- Solids like rock or sand are **denser** than water and sink.  
- Gases are **less dense** than air and rise.  
- Phase interactions (solid/liquid/gas) create dynamic and realistic behaviors.

model.description:
## Hierarchical WebGL Model - Additive Animations and Interactivity

This project presents a **hierarchical WebGL model** demonstrating articulated motion through an **additive animation** system. Each body segment belongs to a parent–child hierarchy, allowing both local and global transformations to combine smoothly in real time.

### Overview

The model features **interactive bone control during playback**. Using rotation sliders, the user can modify joint angles and poses while an animation is running. This approach highlights how additive transformations can be applied dynamically to influence an ongoing animation, producing expressive and customizable motion.

### Features

- **Hierarchical structure** with up to four articulation levels (root > torso > limb > joint)
- **27 degrees of freedom**, allowing a wide range of natural movements
- **Additive animation system**, enabling simultaneous bone manipulation during animation playback
- **Interactive sliders** for adjusting rotation, amplitude, and animation speed
- **UV texture mapping** for detailed surface rendering
- **Blinn–Phong lighting model in view space** for realistic shading with dynamic light control
- **Runtime editing** of parameters such as light position, material properties, and body color

### Objectives

The main goal of this project is to demonstrate how **hierarchical transformations** and **additive motion systems** can be implemented within a low-level WebGL pipeline. It provides insight into how transformation matrices, normal vectors, and lighting equations interact to produce smooth and interactive animations.

### Interactivity

Users can:

- Modify individual bones in real time while an animation is playing
- Adjust light position and intensity dynamically
- Change material and color properties at runtime
- Control animation parameters such as rotation speed and amplitude through sliders

This project highlights the integration of **3D kinematics**, **hierarchical modeling**, and **real-time GPU rendering**, showing how complex articulated models can be animated and controlled interactively using WebGL.

gl_blinn.texture:
## Lighting and Shading

This part of the project focuses on real time lighting and shading. I implemented both **Gouraud shading** and **Phong shading** to compare the two approaches and observe how the lighting calculations affect the final appearance of the mesh.

### Blinn Phong Lighting

The lighting system uses a **Blinn Phong lighting model** based on three main components: ambient, diffuse and specular lighting.

The ambient component provides a base level of illumination. The diffuse component depends on the angle between the surface normal and the light direction. The specular component creates highlights on the surface and is controlled by the shininess value.

The user can interactively modify parameters such as the ambient term, diffuse term, specular term, shininess and light position. This makes it possible to observe how each parameter affects the final appearance of the mesh.

### Gouraud Shading

I implemented **Gouraud shading**, where the lighting calculation is performed in the vertex shader. The resulting colors are then interpolated across the surface by the GPU.

The vertex shader calculates the position and normal of each vertex and uses them for the lighting computation. This produces smooth color transitions across the mesh while keeping the lighting calculation at the vertex level.

### Phong Shading

I also implemented **Phong shading** to compare it with Gouraud shading. With Phong shading, the vertex shader passes the transformed position and normal to the fragment shader. The lighting model is then calculated for each fragment.

This allows the ambient, diffuse and specular components to be calculated for every visible surface point. Compared to Gouraud shading, this can produce more detailed specular highlights across the surface.

## Texture and Mipmapping

The material can switch between two different texture modes depending on the desired result.

### Texture Modes

The first mode uses a **basic albedo color**. In this mode, the mesh is rendered using a simple color without sampling a texture.

The second mode uses a **UV texture**. The UV coordinates of each vertex are passed to the shader and used to sample the texture at the corresponding position.

The fragment shader can use the texture with the following approach:

```glsl
fColor = texture(tex, texcoord) * color;
```

The texture can also be sampled directly when no additional color is required:

```glsl
fColor = texture(tex, texcoord);
```

### Mipmapping

Mipmapping is used to improve texture rendering when a textured object is viewed from a distance. Instead of always using the original texture resolution, smaller versions of the texture can be selected depending on the distance and screen size of the object.

This helps reduce undersampling artifacts and produces more stable texture rendering when the object becomes smaller on screen.
gl_blinn.normal:
## Normal and Shading

This part focuses on the management of normal vectors and the difference between smooth and flat shading.

### Smooth Normals

For smooth shading, the normal of a vertex is calculated using the normals of the faces connected to that vertex. The face normals are averaged to obtain a single vertex normal.

These vertex normals are then interpolated across the surface by the GPU. This produces smooth transitions between adjacent faces and gives the mesh a continuous appearance.

### Flat Normals

For flat shading, each face keeps its own normal instead of sharing averaged vertex normals with adjacent faces. The same normal is therefore used across the whole face.

This produces a faceted appearance and makes the individual polygons of the mesh more visible.

### Shading

The normal vectors are transformed together with the model so that the lighting calculations remain correct after applying the model transformation. The resulting normals can then be used by the lighting system to calculate the diffuse and specular components of the material.
gl_blinn.diagram:
## StaticMesh and OBJ Loading

The **StaticMesh.cpp** class is responsible for loading and interpreting OBJ files. It reads the information contained in each OBJ file and converts it into data that can be used by the rendering system.

### OBJ Data

The loader can retrieve the main elements required to render a mesh, including vertex positions, normal vectors, texture coordinates and face information. This data is then used to construct the corresponding static mesh.

### Mesh and Shader Association

Each OBJ can have its own shader and rendering configuration. This allows different objects in the same scene to use different materials and rendering techniques.

For example, one mesh can use a textured shader while another mesh can use a simple albedo color. The shader and material configuration can therefore be associated with the mesh that is being rendered.

### Rendering Structure

The overall structure separates the loading of the geometry from the rendering process. The OBJ file provides the mesh data, the StaticMesh.cpp class interprets this data, and the selected shader is then used to render the resulting object.

This makes it possible to load multiple OBJ files and render them independently while giving each object its own shader and material settings.

gl_cube.hierarchical:
## Hierarchical bodies

This project is a small 3D scene built with **OpenGL**, focused on the basics of real time rendering and interaction. The scene starts with a simple colored cube and is progressively extended with depth testing, hierarchical transformations, different projection modes, and several rendering effects.

### Features

- **3D colored cube** with six different colored faces
- **Mouse interaction** to rotate the cube
- **Depth buffering** to correctly handle objects in front of or behind each other
- **Display lists** to avoid sending the same geometry commands repeatedly
- **Hierarchical transformations** using the OpenGL matrix stack
- **Animated cube and sphere** attached to the main cube
- **Perspective and orthographic projections** with the ability to switch between them
- **Responsive viewport** that updates when the window is resized
- **Wireframe mode** for displaying the geometry structure
- **Fog effect** with configurable color and distance
- **Alpha blending** to make the main cube partially transparent

### Objectives


The exercises cover depth testing, display lists, matrix stacks, projection transformations, viewport transformations, wireframe rendering, fog, and transparency. The project also introduces hierarchical modeling by attaching several objects to the main cube and animating them through local transformations.

### Interactivity

Users can rotate the main cube with the mouse and switch between different rendering modes. The scene also includes an animated secondary cube and a sphere that follow the transformations of the main object.

The different projection and rendering options make it possible to see how OpenGL handles depth, perspective, transformations, and transparency in a simple interactive 3D scene.
gl_cube.plumbing:
## OpenGL Shaders and Rendering Pipeline

This project introduces the transition from the OpenGL fixed function pipeline to a modern **shader based rendering pipeline** using GLSL. The main focus is on understanding how application data is sent to shaders and how multiple objects can be rendered using different vertex data layouts.

### Features

- **GLSL vertex shaders** using custom vertex attributes and uniforms
- **MVP matrix** combining model, view, and projection transformations
- **GLM** for matrix and camera calculations
- **Mouse controlled cube rotation** through interactive camera and object transformations
- **Multiple objects** rendered using their own transformation matrices
- **Interleaved vertex data** with positions and colors stored in a single VBO
- **Separate VBOs** for position and color data on the octahedron
- **Custom object class** handling the setup and binding of the shader and associated rendering data
- **Reusable rendering structure** that keeps shader setup and object rendering organized
- **VAO and VBO management** for different object data structures


### Object System

A custom **Object class** is used to group the resources and rendering logic associated with each object. The class handles the shader binding and the necessary OpenGL state before drawing, providing a cleaner interface for the main rendering loop.

This structure also makes the rendering code more reusable and reduces unnecessary shader setup when working with multiple objects. Each object can provide its own geometry and transformation while following the same general rendering workflow.

### Rendering Pipeline

For each object, the application binds the required shader and vertex array, computes the object's MVP matrix, sends it to the shader as a uniform, and then issues the draw call.

This creates a clear separation between the application side, which prepares the data and transformations, and the shader side, which processes the vertices on the GPU.

gl_toon.toon:
## Toon Shader

This part of the project focuses on implementing a **toon shader** with a two pass rendering technique. The goal is to create a cartoon like appearance by combining a black outline with discrete lighting levels.

### First Pass: Cel Outline

The first pass is responsible for creating the outline around the model. The vertex shader moves each vertex slightly outwards in the direction of its normal.

Because the vertices are moved away from the original surface, the rendered model becomes slightly larger than the original model. The fragment shader then fills the entire model with black.

When the second pass is rendered on top of the first one, the larger black version remains visible around the edges of the original model, creating the cartoon outline effect.

### Second Pass: Cel Color

The second pass renders the actual model using an illumination model. Instead of keeping the lighting values continuous, the fragment shader converts the gradual light intensities into a small number of discrete levels.

This is done using a step function, which creates clear transitions between different lighting levels. The result is a stylized appearance similar to traditional cartoon rendering.

The combination of the black outline from the first pass and the discrete lighting from the second pass produces the final toon shading effect.
gl_toon.postprocess:
## Post Processing

This part of the project focuses on applying image processing effects to the rendered scene. Instead of directly displaying the 3D scene, the result can first be rendered to a texture and then processed using another shader.

### Shader Texture

The **shaderTex** program is used to render a texture directly to the screen. The vertex shader receives the coordinates of a fullscreen quad and converts them from the range of -1 to 1 into UV coordinates from 0 to 1.

The fragment shader then receives these UV coordinates and can calculate the final color of each pixel. A time value can also be passed to the shader, allowing animated effects to be created based on the current time.

### Texture to Screen

The rendered image can be displayed using a fullscreen quad. The viewport and buffers are cleared before using the shader, then the quad is rendered with a triangle strip.

This technique allows the texture containing the rendered scene to be displayed and processed as a regular image.

### Frame Buffer

A **Frame Buffer Object**, also called an FBO, is used as an offscreen rendering destination. It works like a hidden screen where the scene can be rendered before being displayed on the actual screen.

The framebuffer can contain different types of buffers:

- **Color buffer**, stored as a texture and used to store the rendered image
- **Depth buffer**, used to store depth information
- **Stencil buffer**, used for stencil operations

A framebuffer can contain multiple color buffers when several rendering outputs are required. The depth and stencil buffers are stored using render buffer objects.

### Post Processing Effects

Once the scene has been rendered into a texture, different effects can be applied to the resulting image:

- **Blur**, used to soften the image by averaging neighboring pixels
- **Pixelize**, used to create a pixelated visual effect
- **Grayscale**, used to remove color information and convert the image to grayscale
- **Passthrough**, which displays the original image without modifying it
- **Sobel Filter**, used to detect edges and highlight contours in the rendered image

### Sobel Filter

The **Sobel filter** is an image processing technique commonly used for edge detection. It analyzes the differences between neighboring pixels to detect strong changes in color or intensity.

This makes it possible to highlight the contours and edges of objects in the rendered image. The filter can therefore be used as another post processing effect to emphasize the structure of the scene.

### Cleanup

Framebuffers and their associated resources need to be properly destroyed when they are no longer required. The resources used by the framebuffer are cleaned up at the end of the rendering process:

- **Rendered texture**
- **Depth render buffer**
- **Framebuffer**

This prevents unused GPU resources from remaining allocated.

gl_pengine.description:
## Physics Engine in OpenGL

This project is a 3D physics engine developed in **OpenGL**, divided into multiple interactive scenes. It demonstrates fundamental physics principles, particle dynamics, spring forces, collision detection algorithms, and numerical integration methods.

### Featured Scenes

- **Simple Particle Projection**: Particle motion with mass, velocity, and drag
- **Magnetized Particles**: Charged particles following Coulomb law
- **Spring System**: Spring force simulation with configurable stiffness
- **AABB Collisions**: Collision detection using broad and narrow phases
- **Halfspace Collision**: Objects contained in a moving box bounded by halfspaces
- **RK4 Integration**: Pendulum simulation comparing classic Euler progression with the RK4 algorithm
gl_pengine.particle:
## Simple Particle Projection

This scene demonstrates simple particle motion in a 3D environment. Particles are launched into the scene and interact with basic physical properties.

### Features

- **Mass**: Each particle has an individual mass affecting its acceleration
- **Initial Velocity**: Custom launching vectors for speed and direction
- **Drag Force**: Air resistance applied to simulate realistic trajectory decay

### Objectives

The main goal of this scene is to establish the baseline particle motion equation and observe how velocity, gravity, and drag forces combine to form parabolic trajectories.
gl_pengine.mag:
## Magnetized Particles

This scene introduces charged particles governed by **Coulomb law**. The environment contains positive and negative charges that interact dynamically with each other and static field sources.

### Features

- **Opposing Charges**: Red particles represent positive charges and blue particles represent negative charges
- **Coulomb Force**: Particles exert attractive or repulsive forces based on their charge magnitude and distance
- **Attractors and Repellers**: Blue particles are attracted to a central white point while red particles are repelled

### Behavior

The interaction between particle charges and the central attractor creates complex orbital patterns and dynamic particle clusters.
gl_pengine.spring:
## Spring Force Simulation

This scene demonstrates spring dynamics using the **Spring Force Formula** (Hooke law). It compares how different stiffness values affect stability and motion.

### Features

- **Hooke Law**: Spring force calculation based on displacement and stiffness coefficient **k**
- **Stiffness Comparison**: Side by side scenarios comparing low stiffness (soft spring) and high stiffness (rigid spring)
- **Realistic Motion**: Smooth oscillations with dampening forces applied over time

### Behavior

The simulation showcases how spring stiffness influences oscillation frequency and amplitude, producing realistic elastic behaviors.
gl_pengine.aabb:
## AABB Collision Detection

This scene focuses on collision detection between particles and bounding volumes using **Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes** (AABB).

### Collision Phases

- **Broad Phase**: Quick spatial test to filter out distant objects and reduce unnecessary calculations
- **Narrow Phase**: Precise bounding box intersection test to detect exact collision points and normals
- **Particle Dynamics**: Particles have different sizes and masses, resulting in varied fall speeds and bounce patterns
gl_pengine.half:
## Halfspace Collision and Enclosed Environment

This scene features particles enclosed inside a moving box made of **halfspaces**, operating under high gravity and drag forces.

### Halfspace Mechanics

- **Definition**: A halfspace is an infinite plane where the entire region behind the plane is treated as a solid volume
- **Contact Normal**: When an object interpenetrates a halfspace, the contact normal always points in the direction of the plane normal, even if the object is entirely behind the plane
- **Moving Container**: The outer box can move and rotate, continuously updating the halfspace planes and forcing particles to react to the moving walls
gl_pengine.rk4:
## Numerical Integration: RK4 vs Frame Progression

This scene presents a multi-segment pendulum with high spring stiffness, comparing standard frame progression against the **Runge-Kutta 4th Order (RK4)** integration algorithm.

### Comparison

- **Euler / Frame Progression**: Standard linear integration leads to energy accumulation, jittery motion, and instability when high forces are applied
- **RK4 Integration**: Evaluates four intermediate steps per frame to approximate higher-order derivatives, delivering smooth, realistic, and stable simulation even with extremely high stiffness values

### Results

The RK4 method prevents numerical explosion and maintains physical stability throughout complex multi-body constraint chains.

gl_raycast.description:
## Raycasting Engine and BRDF Shading

This project is a **raycasting engine** developed inside the fragment shader using OpenGL. It renders 3D scenes containing various geometric surfaces (planes, spheres, and triangle meshes) by solving ray intersections using the equation r(t) = o + td, where t represents the intersection distance.

### Architecture and Performance

- **Shader Storage Buffer Objects (SSBOs)**: Used in the fragment shader instead of Uniform Buffers (UBOs) to overcome memory size limitations and ensure scalability with large numbers of objects
- **Multiple View Modes**: Toggle between Normal view, Depth view, and Lit view
- **Geometric Intersections**: Specialized Ray-Sphere, Ray-Plane, and Ray-TriangleMesh functions with full occlusion handling

### BRDF Lighting and Shading

- **Lighting Components**: Support for ambient, diffuse, and specular terms
- **Dual Specular Models**: Implementation of both Phong and Blinn-Phong specular models
- **Shadow Rendering**: Support for both hard and soft shadows with shadow acne removal
- **Visual Quality**: Built-in antialiasing to smooth object edges

### Interactivity

- **Movable Camera**: Orbital camera movement around objects in the 3D scene
- **Movable Light Source**: Interactive light positioning to observe dynamic shading and shadow transitions
gl_raycast.aal:
## Antialiasing and Supersampling

Antialiasing is a technique used to reduce the appearance of jagged edges. The renderer relies on supersampling to produce smooth image contours.

### Implementation Details

- **Supersampling**: Casts multiple rays through each image pixel using a _SAMPLE_RATE_ of 16
- **Color Averaging**: Computes the final pixel color by averaging the contribution of all sample rays
- **Edge Smoothing**: Reduces aliasing artifacts along geometry boundaries.
gl_raycast.spec:
## Specular Term: Phong and Blinn-Phong

This project implements both Phong and Blinn-Phong specular models to evaluate surface highlights.

### Model Comparison

- **Phong Model**: Calculates specular highlights using the light reflection vector and the view direction
- **Blinn-Phong Model**: Modifies the Phong model by introducing the halfway vector, a unit vector placed exactly halfway between the view direction and the light direction
- **Visual Results**: Simplifies shading calculations while providing smoother and more consistent specular highlights.

gl_raytrace.description:
## Recursive Raytracer and Complex Materials

This project implements a **recursive raytracing algorithm** directly within a fragment shader. The scene contains 4 spheres with varying reflection and refraction properties to simulate realistic transparent materials like glass and water.

### Fresnel Effect

- **Combined Reflection and Refraction**: Real transparent materials exhibit both refractive and reflective behaviors
- **Angle-Dependent Reflectivity**: Reflectivity increases as the viewing angle shifts from perpendicular (aligned with the normal) to parallel (orthogonal to the normal)

### Beer's Law Absorption

- **Light Attenuation**: Light is absorbed and scattered as it travels through a medium
- **Distance-Based Decay**: The total attenuation along the ray depends directly on the distance traveled inside the material
gl_raytrace.spheres:
## Ray-Sphere Intersection

The spheres share the same intersection logic as the raycasting engine. Rays are modeled using the equation r(t) = o + td, and the exact intersection point is found by solving for t.

gpu_julia.description:
## Julia Set Fractals on GPU

This project provides a real time visualization of Julia set fractals calculated directly on the GPU.

### Features

- **GPU Parallel Computing**: Accelerates fractal calculations for every pixel on screen
- **Real Time Rendering**: Smooth visualization of complex Julia set patterns

gpu_gol.description:
## Conway Game of Life on GPU (CUDA)

This project implements Conway's Game of Life, a cellular automaton where a grid of cells evolves through discrete time steps based on neighbor states.

### CUDA Implementation

- **2D Parallel Grid**: Cell state updates are processed directly inside a CUDA kernel
- **High Performance**: Enables real time simulation of large grids by leveraging GPU architecture

gpu_raytracing.description:
## GPU Raytracing

This project implements a GPU-based raytracing approach by simulating a virtual camera within a 3D scene.

### Features

- **Light Sensor Model**: Determines the light hitting each sensor point on the camera to form the final image
- **Movable Camera**: Vertical and horizontal camera movement within the 3D space
